title: Debugging a Running Container
intro: Beyond logs and exec, Docker has several inspection tools for figuring out exactly what's happening inside a running container without guessing.

steps.prompt: Check live CPU/memory usage of all running containers.
steps.fake_output:
CONTAINER ID   NAME   CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT
a1b2c3d4       web    142.3%  890MiB / 512MiB
steps.explanation: 142% CPU across multiple cores is fine, but MEM USAGE exceeding the LIMIT (890MiB used against a 512MiB limit) means this container is at serious risk of getting OOM-killed.
steps.why: This is the Docker equivalent of 'kubectl top pods' — live resource usage, not the static limits configured at run time. Add a container name/id as an argument to stop it from refreshing every container and focus on just one.

steps.prompt: See the actual processes running inside the 'web' container.
steps.fake_output:
UID    PID    PPID   CMD
root   4821   4801   node server.js
root   4855   4821   node worker.js
steps.explanation: This shows processes from the HOST's perspective, using the host's process table — it works even if the container has no shell to exec into.
steps.why: 'docker exec web ps aux' shows almost the same thing but requires the container to actually have a working shell and ps binary — minimal/distroless images often have neither, which is exactly when 'docker top' becomes the only option.

steps.prompt: Check environment variables actually set inside the running container.
steps.explanation: This shows what's ACTUALLY set at runtime — useful when a value from your .env file or docker-compose.yml doesn't seem to be taking effect.
steps.why: The Dockerfile's ENV instructions, a docker run -e flag, and a Compose environment: block can all set the same variable — if a value looks wrong, checking it live inside the running container is the fastest way to see which of those actually won, without tracing through every config file.

steps.prompt: Check the exact exit code the last time this container stopped.
steps.explanation: 137 specifically means the container was killed by SIGKILL (137 = 128 + 9) — almost always an OOM kill, matching what 'docker stats' showed earlier about exceeding its memory limit.
steps.why: --format lets you pull one specific field out of inspect's huge JSON blob instead of scrolling through everything — same idea as kubectl's -o jsonpath, just using Go template syntax instead.

steps.prompt: Watch the live stream of Docker daemon events (container starts, stops, kills) as they happen.
steps.fake_output:
2026-09-27T10:00:01 container die web (exitCode=137)
2026-09-27T10:00:03 container start web
steps.explanation: This confirms the restart policy actually kicked in and restarted the container after the OOM kill — 'die' followed by 'start' a couple seconds later.
steps.why: This is a live stream, not a snapshot — it's what you'd run in a second terminal while reproducing a flaky crash, to catch the exact moment and reason a container goes down, rather than piecing it together after the fact from logs alone.
